The Statue.
A shoebill can stand almost perfectly still for more than half an hour,
bill pointed down at the water, without giving the fish a single reason to look up.
It hunts by sight alone, so it either stands and waits,
or it wades forward so slowly that it barely counts as walking.
It can hold still longer than a waiter pretending he hasn't seen you.

The Bill.
The shoebill's bill can be twenty-four centimeters long,
the third-longest of any living bird, behind only the pelicans and the largest storks.
It is shaped like a giant wooden shoe, which is the whole reason for the name,
and in Sudan it was known in Arabic as abu markub, father of the shoe.
It is nearly as long as a man's shoe, except this shoe has sharp edges and a hook on the end.

The Floating Mat.
To fish in deep water, the shoebill needs something to stand on,
so it walks out onto floating mats of plants.
A bird as tall as a child weighs only four to seven kilograms,
and the mats are all it needs.
Its stronghold is the Sudd in South Sudan, a vast swamp on the White Nile,
where the protected wetland alone covers fifty-seven thousand square kilometers
and more shoebills live than anywhere else.
It avoids solid walls of papyrus, which are too thick to fish in,

The Water Bucket.
When the swamp heats up, a shoebill parent fills its bill with water,
carries it home, and pours it over the eggs,

Shoebills usually lay two eggs, and the second one can arrive up to five days after the first.
